Newly released cydippid larvae of the sea gooseberry Pleurobrachia pileus emerge from the egg with a polar length measured at only 0.0226 centimeters [Lb = 0.0226 centimeters], a diminutive size that marks the onset of the free-swimming planktonic stage. At an experimental temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], these tiny larvae undergo their trophic switch and commence exogenous feeding remarkably quickly, with the interval from fertilization to first prey capture lasting approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days]. This rapid onset of feeding is a critical life-history transition, as it determines the timing of subsequent growth and development during the planktonic phase. The initial diameter of the newly hatched individual is even more minute, approximately 0.0125 cm, though the polar length provides a more consistent metric for morphological comparison across developmental stages.

As the post-metamorphic juvenile grows through successive molts and allometric shifts, it eventually approaches a maximum polar length of 3.1 cm [Li = 3.1 cm], a value that represents the asymptotic size of the adult body form. This ultimate polar length is attained only after the organism has passed through a distinctive period of accelerated somatic growth following the larval-juvenile transition. In laboratory cultures maintained at stable temperatures of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the total duration from hatching to senescence spans approximately 250 days [am = approximately 250 days], a lifespan that places this species among the shorter-lived members of the ctenophore community. This maximum longevity is constrained by both metabolic demands and reproductive investment, as the organism channels considerable resources into gamete production rather than extended somatic maintenance.

Reproductive maturation in Pleurobrachia pileus is marked by the attainment of a specific polar length when the gonads first become active. Field surveys and laboratory observations consistently indicate that puberty occurs once the individual reaches a polar length of 0.69 centimeters [Lp = 0.69 centimeters]. At this stage of sexual maturation, the organism is capable of initiating gametogenesis, but peak reproductive effort is typically deferred until somatic growth has progressed further. The post-pubertal adult gradually shifts its energy budget from somatic investment toward the production of gametes, and it is during this period that the highest daily egg output is observed. The relationship between body size and reproductive potential is tightly coupled, with larger females producing disproportionately more eggs per unit time.

At a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], fully mature individuals can sustain a remarkable maximum reproductive rate of 1196 eggs per day [Ri = 1196 eggs per day], an output that reflects the species' strategy of high fecundity typical of gelatinous zooplankton. This prodigious daily egg production is driven by the continuous maturation of oocytes within the gonadal canals, and the spawning events occur daily once the female reaches reproductive maturity. For comparison, Greve (1972) documented an even higher output of 7075 eggs per day for a single 15 mm individual under potentially more optimal conditions, though the value of 1196 eggs per day at 10 °C [T = 10 °C] is considered representative for animals cultured at lower thermal regimes that slow ovarian turnover.

The respiratory quotient measured for Pleurobrachia pileus under routine metabolic conditions stands at 0.74 , a value that indicates a predominantly lipid-based catabolic fuel during periods of active foraging and growth. This reliance on lipid oxidation is consistent with the high energy density of the copepod prey that constitutes the majority of the diet. At the asymptotic size of 3.1 cm [Li = 3.1 cm] in polar length, the estimated ultimate dry weight of a fully grown individual is 0.394 grams , derived from the length-weight relationship established by Mutlu and Bingel (1999). The dry mass of 0.394 grams is consistent with the high reproductive investment of gelatinous zooplankton, where body reserves are channeled primarily into gamete production rather than structural maintenance, reflecting a trade-off that favours fecundity over extended lifespan.
